deduped_items.title: EU Acknowledges Concerns Over Asbestos Contamination
deduped_items.summary: The European Commission acknowledges the seriousness of concerns over asbestos contamination in Hungary, the head of the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Environment informed Laurie Kazan-Allen, coordinator of an international organization advocating an asbestos ban. The letter was forwarded to MTI on Thursday by Dániel Holdosi, an activist from Szombathely. François Wakenhut was responding to an open […] The post EU Acknowledges Concerns Over Asbestos Contamination appeared first o
deduped_items.body_text:
Temporary chemical measures on affected roads must not distract from the fact that the government still lacks a genuine and transparent action plan.Continue reading
The European Commission acknowledges the seriousness of concerns over asbestos contamination in Hungary, the head of the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Environment informed Laurie Kazan-Allen, coordinator of an international organization advocating an asbestos ban. The letter was forwarded to MTI on Thursday by Dániel Holdosi, an activist from Szombathely.
François Wakenhut was responding to an open letter written in early July by 14 international anti-asbestos occupational safety, health, and environmental protection organizations and experts to the leaders of the European Union and Hungary.
In the document, they drew attention to the gravity of the situation in Szombathely, highlighting the dangers posed by the contamination, posing a particular threat to children’s health.
In a letter written on behalf of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the director-general emphasized that it is primarily the responsibility of the competent national authorities to ensure compliance with applicable EU rules in such cases, to assess the risks, and to take the necessary protective and remediation measures.
The European Commission is confident that the national authorities will continue to act swiftly and decisively to protect public health in the affected areas,”
François Wakenhut stated.
The asbestos contamination scandal broke out the day after Hungary’s parliamentary elections, when in Vas County the head of the environmental protection department at the local government office and the mayor of Szombathely announced at an emergency press conference that, in one of the city’s single-family residential areas, on several streets of the “Oladi Plateau,” crushed stone containing asbestos had been spread years earlier. Airborne asbestos fibers are seriously harmful to health.
István Orbán, director general of the government office, said that, according to reports, four quarries in Burgenland, Austria, had previously been closed due to high asbestos content, and they suspect the material may have come from there.
András Nemény, mayor of Szombathely, announced that 12 kilometers of streets in that part of the city are covered with asbestos-contaminated crushed stone, and the cost of safely removing and disposing of it exceeds the city’s financial resources.
To access the force majeure fund, he appealed to both the outgoing government and the incoming government for assistance. Tibor Navracsics, the outgoing Minister of Regional Development, promised to make the fund available, and a supporting government resolution was passed, but only the local government was able to take concrete steps; to prevent dust from spreading, they began regularly watering the affected streets and even applied a layer of bitumen to some sections, while awaiting guidance from experts on exactly what steps to take.
In the following weeks, several municipalities in Vas County—including Kőszeg, Lukácsháza, Bük, and Sárvár—reported that they might also be affected; laboratory tests revealed asbestos levels exceeding the threshold in all of these locations.
In Táplánszentkereszt, the areas in front of the daycare center, kindergarten, and school were inadvertently covered with asbestos-containing material; there, too, the local government had no other option but to spray the area with calcium chloride. In Bük, the local government had the material removed at its own expense, in compliance with regulations governing hazardous materials.
In Szombathely, weekly public forums were held; construction in the area was halted due to the imposed restrictions, and heavy vehicle traffic was temporarily banned and then restricted during certain periods.
On May 21, the Hungarian prime minister held talks in Vienna with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.
They announced that a joint Hungarian

deduped_items.body_text:
Foreign Pupils on the Rise in Czech Schools - Nearly One in Five in Prague
Prague Morning
Of the nearly one million pupils attending Czech primary schools last academic year, almost 8% were foreign nationals, most commonly from Ukraine.
According to the Czech Statistical Office (CSO), Prague recorded the highest proportion, with foreign pupils making up 18% of all children in its primary schools.
Compulsory education is mandatory for Czech citizens as well as citizens of other European Union member states who reside in the Czech Republic for more than 90 days. The requirement also applies to foreign nationals with long-term residence permits.
Their children therefore have the same rights as Czech children, including access to free education, school meals and extracurricular activities.
The number of foreign pupils increased significantly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, nearly doubling that year. Their numbers have continued to rise ever since. Today, children from Ukraine account for 5% of all pupils in the Czech Republic.
The trend is similar in secondary schools, where the proportion of foreign pupils reached its highest level in the past 10 years, at almost 5% of the total.
Although the number of children in primary schools has remained relatively stable at just over one million in recent years, a sharp decline is expected in the coming years due to the falling birth rate, according to Vendula Kašparová of the CSO’s Social Development Statistics Department. The office said the birth rate has been falling continuously for the fifth consecutive year.
The decline is already visible at the kindergarten level. The number of children enrolled in kindergartens fell below 350,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, the first time this has happened since 2013. Over the past three years, enrolment has dropped by more than 21,000 children, or around 5.8%.
Fewer Children Receiving Deferrals From Starting School
Kašparová identifies another clear trend: fewer children are being granted deferrals from starting compulsory school. Since the 2021/2022 academic year, the proportion of six-year-olds whose school entry was deferred has fallen from 24.1% in September 2021 to 17.7% in September 2025, representing just under 21,000 pupils.
Furthermore, an amendment to the Education Act is expected to reduce the number of deferrals even further. Under the new rules, deferrals will only be granted when justified by a medical condition that prevents a child from attending school.
This could include a serious medical condition following surgery, cancer treatment or a moderate intellectual disability.

deduped_items.body_text:
Czechia, the Land of Burgers. More Fast Food Chains Enter the Market
Prague Morning
The Czech fast food market is expanding beyond its established players, with new international brands entering the country and existing chains opening restaurants in smaller cities.
McDonald’s and KFC continue to build their networks, while brands from Germany, the United States and Poland are looking for opportunities in the Czech Republic.
The expansion is increasingly moving beyond Prague and other major cities, with retail parks becoming an important location for new restaurants.
Burgermeister prepares Czech debut
One of the newest international brands preparing to enter the Czech market is Germany’s Burgermeister. The Berlin-based burger chain plans to open its first restaurant on Wenceslas Square at the beginning of next year.
The company already sees its Prague location as more than a single restaurant. It is also considering further locations across the country.
Popeyes and Burger King continue expanding
Burger King entered the Czech market 18 years ago and now operates around 70 restaurants. Popeyes arrived much later but has expanded quickly, opening 19 locations during its first three years in the country.
The companies are building a network that stretches from smaller regional towns to central Prague. In Králův Dvůr, a town of around 11,000 people, both Burger King and Popeyes operate at the Litavka Retail Park.
Popeyes is preparing additional restaurants at the Eden shopping centre and in the Budějovická area of Prague. The chain is also expanding into regional cities, with planned locations in Klatovy and Písek.
Five Guys adds another international brand
The Czech burger market gained another major international name last December when U.S. chain Five Guys opened its first Prague restaurant.
The restaurant is located in the former Máj department store on Národní Street. Five Guys is known for burgers prepared to order and a wide range of toppings, allowing customers to customise their meals.
Its prices, however, are generally higher than those of traditional fast food chains.
Another U.S. brand, Dave’s Hot Chicken, is also expected to enter the Czech market this year, according to consulting firm Cushman & Wakefield.
The chain specialises in spicy fried chicken and will therefore compete directly with established players such as KFC and Popeyes.
Czech chains are looking beyond their home cities
The expansion is not limited to international companies.
Czech burger chain Mama’s Burger is also developing its network. Originally based in Ostrava, the company has expanded into several larger Czech cities and operates a restaurant at Prague’s Arkády Pankrác shopping centre.
The company is also seeking franchise partners as it looks to increase the number of locations.

deduped_items.body_text:
Slavia Prague to Face Bayern Munich, Arsenal and Porto in Champions League
Prague Morning
Slavia Prague have learned their eight opponents for the 2026/27 UEFA Champions League league phase following Thursday’s draw in Monaco.
Slavia will play four matches at home at Eden Arena and four away.
At home, Slavia will welcome Arsenal, Aston Villa, Villarreal and Lens. Their away fixtures will take them to Bayern Munich, Porto, Fenerbahçe and Sabah Baku in Azerbaijan.
The most high-profile home fixture will be against Arsenal, the reigning Premier League champions. Slavia also faced the London club in last season’s Champions League campaign, making the return meeting at Eden Arena particularly notable.
The toughest away assignment is likely to come in Munich, where Slavia will face six-time European champions Bayern at the Allianz Arena. The team will also travel to Portugal to meet Porto and to Istanbul for a match against Fenerbahçe.
The longest trip of the league phase will be to Baku to face Azerbaijani champions Sabah, who are making their debut in the Champions League league phase.
How the Champions League league phase works
The 2026/27 competition is being played under UEFA’s new league-phase format for the third consecutive season. Instead of a traditional group stage, all 36 teams are placed in one league table.
Each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents, with two opponents drawn from each of the four seeding pots. Every team has four home and four away games.
The top eight teams in the final standings will advance directly to the round of 16. Teams finishing ninth to 24th will enter a knockout playoff for the remaining eight places, while clubs finishing from 25th to 36th will be eliminated.
The league phase begins on September 8–10, with six rounds taking place before the end of 2026. The final two matchdays will be played in January, with the league phase concluding on January 27. UEFA will announce the exact dates and kick-off times for each individual match later.

deduped_items.body_text:
‘Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang,’ ‘Sister Stella L’ to lead PFIM 2026 screenings
With the theme “Pelikula: Ginintuang Ikalawa,” this year’s celebration of the Philippine Film Industry Month (PFIM) will feature screenings of digitally restored classics including Lino Brocka’s “Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang” and Mike de Leon’s “Sister Stella L,” among others.
The Film Development Council of the Philippines (FDCP) announced PFIM’s monthlong activities that celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Second Golden Age of Philippine Cinema.
The screening of “Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang” will kick off the celebration at the Red Carpet Cinema, Shangri-La Plaza on Sept. 4, along with the announcement of the Philippines’ entry to the 2027 Oscars Best International Feature Film category.
Other digitally restored classics — including de Leon’s “Itim,” Brocka’s “Insiang,” Mario O’Hara’s “Tatlong Taong Walang Diyos,” Lupita Aquino-Kashiwahara’s “Minsa’y Isang Gamu-Gamo,” Eddie Romero’s “Ganito Kami Noon… Paano Kayo Ngayon?” and Ishmael Bernal’s “Nunal sa Tubig” — will be showcased throughout the month at FDCP Cinematheque Centres nationwide.
The audiences will also be taken further back in time with the “SineUna: Cinematic Action Before the War,” which will feature Eduardo de Castro’s “Zamboanga,” Carlos Vander Tolosa’s “Giliw Ko,” Vicente Salumbide’s “Ibong Adarna” and Octavio Silos’ “Tunay na Ina” and “Pakiusap.”
Meanwhile, the newly digitally-restored “Sister Stella L” will have its grand homecoming on Sept. 20 at the Metropolitan Theater as part of the “Mga Hiyas ng Sineng Pilipino,” which is co-presented by the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA).
READ: FDCP sets 1st Nat’l Cinema Day in Sept. with aim to bring audiences back to theaters
Other key PFIM 2026 events include the “Reel to Real: Pelikula at Panayam,” which will spotlight Brocka’s “Jaguar”; the Director’s Series, which will feature Jeffrey Jeturian’s “Tuhog” and “Kubrador”; the world premiere of Mike Alcazaren’s documentary film “Kodomo-tachi: Children of the War” on Sept. 17; the inaugural edition of the PFIM Short Film Competition; Sine Kabataan 2026; and the return of the Film Education Convention (FilmEc).
The PFIM 2026 will conclude with a closing ceremony on Sept. 30. /ra

deduped_items.body_text:
Sarah Geronimo madbos? Matteo nakadawat og ‘soon-to-be daddy’ greeting
Mga netizens naghunahuna nga mabdos si Sarah Geronimo human ang iyang asawa, ang aktor nga si Matteo Guidicelli, nakadawat og “soon-to-be daddy” congratulatory greeting sa usa ka nagpa-ila nga amigo.
Usa ka Facebook user, nga amigo ni Guidicelli, ang nag-post og hulagway nila sa aktor nga karon gi-delete na. Matod pa niya, kuha ang maong photo dihang nag-abot sila sa usa ka coffee shop sa Quezon City
“Deep in a meeting with a colleague, totally unaware someone familiar was right there until Gianmatteo Guidecilli walked up and said, ‘ka-ila gyud ko ani!’ (I know this person!)” segon pa sa giingon amigo. “Truly caught me by surprise! So many shared memories with Matt —from shoots, Airborne Proficiency Jumps, and our days at ISAFP. Solid guy — hindi mayabang, sobrang friendly pa.”
READ: Sarah Geronimo reunites with mom Divine, dad Delfin for her 38th birthday
(Sa ka focus nako sa usa ka meeting sa akong kauban, wala ko kabantay nga naa koy kaiila nga naa sa [cafe] hangtod nidoul siya ug nag-sulti, ‘Ka-ila man gyod ko ani! […] Tinoud nakuratan ko! Daghan kaayo mig kaagi ni Matt — gikan sa mga shoots, Airborne Proficiency Jumps, ug sa among mga adlaw sa ISAFP. Saligan gyud na nga tawo — di hambugero, ug friendly pa gyod kaayo.)
READ: Sarah Geronimo bonds with dad Delfin for the first time in years
“P.S. He is soon to be a daddy. Congratulations, bro!” sulti pas user. (Hapit na siya mahimong daddy. Pahalipay, bro!)
Gitubag sab sa maong user ang usa sa mga komento sa iyang post, diin giingon niya nga si Guidicelli mismo ang miingon ug nagkumpirma nga mabdos si Geronimo.
Sarah Geronimo, Matteo Guidicelli hilom pa
Sa pagkaron, si Guidicelli ug Geronimo — nga nagpakasal niadtong 2020 — wala pa mohatag og kumpirmasyon o pag-deny sa mga tsismis bahin sa pagmabdos.
READ: Matteo Guidicelli vows to be better husband to Sarah Geronimo on 12th anniversary
Ang aktres ug singer nagsaulog sa iyang ika-38 nga adlaw nga natawhan pinaagi sa pagpakig-uban pag-usab sa iyang mga ginikanan nga sila Delfin ug Divine Geronimo.

deduped_items.body_text:
‘Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang,’ ‘Sister Stella L’ to lead PFIM 2026 screenings
With the theme “Pelikula: Ginintuang Ikalawa,” this year’s celebration of the Philippine Film Industry Month (PFIM) will feature screenings of digitally restored classics including Lino Brocka’s “Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang” and Mike de Leon’s “Sister Stella L,” among others.
The Film Development Council of the Philippines (FDCP) announced PFIM’s monthlong activities that celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Second Golden Age of Philippine Cinema.
The screening of “Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang” will kick off the celebration at the Red Carpet Cinema, Shangri-La Plaza on Sept. 4, along with the announcement of the Philippines’ entry to the 2027 Oscars Best International Feature Film category.
Other digitally restored classics — including de Leon’s “Itim,” Brocka’s “Insiang,” Mario O’Hara’s “Tatlong Taong Walang Diyos,” Lupita Aquino-Kashiwahara’s “Minsa’y Isang Gamu-Gamo,” Eddie Romero’s “Ganito Kami Noon… Paano Kayo Ngayon?” and Ishmael Bernal’s “Nunal sa Tubig” — will be showcased throughout the month at FDCP Cinematheque Centres nationwide.
The audiences will also be taken further back in time with the “SineUna: Cinematic Action Before the War,” which will feature Eduardo de Castro’s “Zamboanga,” Carlos Vander Tolosa’s “Giliw Ko,” Vicente Salumbide’s “Ibong Adarna” and Octavio Silos’ “Tunay na Ina” and “Pakiusap.”
Meanwhile, the newly digitally-restored “Sister Stella L” will have its grand homecoming on Sept. 20 at the Metropolitan Theater as part of the “Mga Hiyas ng Sineng Pilipino,” which is co-presented by the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA).
READ: FDCP sets 1st Nat’l Cinema Day in Sept. with aim to bring audiences back to theaters
Other key PFIM 2026 events include the “Reel to Real: Pelikula at Panayam,” which will spotlight Brocka’s “Jaguar”; the Director’s Series, which will feature Jeffrey Jeturian’s “Tuhog” and “Kubrador”; the world premiere of Mike Alcazaren’s documentary film “Kodomo-tachi: Children of the War” on Sept. 17; the inaugural edition of the PFIM Short Film Competition; Sine Kabataan 2026; and the return of the Film Education Convention (FilmEc).
The PFIM 2026 will conclude with a closing ceremony on Sept. 30. /ra
deduped_items.normalised_title: tinimbang ka ngunit kulang sister stella l to lead pfim 2026 screenings

deduped_items.title: FULL INTERVIEW: Mike Dizon on drumming for 3 bands, love for food
deduped_items.summary: Dizon sits down with Rappler to talk about his beginnings in music, what it's like for him to move from genre to genre as the drummer of TEETH, Sandwich, and Pedicab, and how he discovered his love for documenting the restaurants he comes across
deduped_items.body_text:
MANILA, Philippines – It’s not every day that an artist finds himself being a part of three of the Philippines’ most influential bands at the same time, until you meet Mike Dizon.
Dizon co-founded the alternative rock and grunge outfit TEETH in 1993. Years later, he also began playing the drums for rock band Sandwich and electronic rock band Pedicab. He is also a prolific songwriter, and is the mind behind hit songs like “Laklak” and “Prinsesa” by TEETH.
Outside of music, though, Dizon runs a successful YouTube channel, where he visits local eateries to try out the best dishes on the menu.
Ahead of TEETH’s reunion concert tour in celebration of their 33 years as a band, Dizon sits down with Rappler to talk about his beginnings in music, what it’s like for him to move from genre to genre, and how he discovered his love for documenting the restaurants he comes across.
Catch the full interview at 7 pm on Saturday, August 29, by bookmarking this page or heading to Rappler’s YouTube! – Rappler.com

deduped_items.body_text:
Rescuers in Nepal and China were battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing entire villages.
The latest figures from both countries put the number of missing close to 3,000, with 633 bodies recovered — and reports of some dead possibly swept downstream as far away as India.
Rescue worker Kawan Koirala, from the Nepal Scout Disaster Response Team, said they were struggling in thick, leg-sucking mud.
“People want their want their family’s body back, either dead or alive, but we cannot find them… you can see the mud,” he told AFP, exhausted after an 18 hour shift.
“It is very traumatic for me too. It is my first time seeing these types of things. Everywhere is mud. We faced floods in Nepal before, but not like this.”
The US Geological Survey said the disaster on Wednesday on the Tibet-Nepal border was caused by a glacial collapse that created a torrent of debris downstream.
Those that made it out say they have lost everything and now face an agonising wait to discover the fate of missing loved ones, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away. There is nothing left,” survivor Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP.
“There is nothing left.”
At Bidur’s army base, a key rescue hub in the same district, relatives crowded around lists of rescued people pasted on a wall.
Samjhana Thing said she had been waiting three days for news of her missing brother.
“We don’t know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place,” she said.
“I have come here looking for my son,” said Kalka Sharda, scanning the list in desperation.
“He was a labourer at the hydropower plant, but I can’t find his name, and the authorities are not saying anything.”
In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority listed 933 hydropower workers among the missing, along with 517 foreigners, including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
Risk of lake burst near disaster site wanes
The threat of a lake formed after the glacier collapse has eased, Chinese authorities said on Saturday, as it appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday to Saturday morning suggest that water in the lake, which straddles the border between China’s Tibet region and Nepal at the confluence of two rivers, has been slowly flowing out and gradually reducing the reservoir, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the Water Resources Ministry.
By Saturday afternoon, parts of the lake bed had become visible, CCTV reported.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the lake on the Purepu Tsangpo river showed it covered 99,000 square metres early on Saturday, roughly the size of 14 soccer pitches, having shrunk by 21,000 square metres since Thursday.
‘Enormous’ trauma
The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous”, and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise.
Emergency teams worked flat out to find survivors as widespread devastation left communities short of food and water.
Fears of further flooding have compounded the search for the missing.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes, and one of these formations has become a risk of further floods.
While the exact cause of the collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of such disasters.
In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing had paused its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding.
On the Nepali side, soldiers were trying desperately to drill through to 100 people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project on Saturday.
The prime minister’s office said teams had begun “clearing mud and debris” to open the entrance, while a specialised Indian tunnel rescue unit had arrived to help.

deduped_items.title: Population to plummet, council warns
deduped_items.body_text:
- 
            Population to plummet, council warnsINCREASING IMBALANCE: The percentage of working-age people is expected to shrink to 42.3% of the population, while older people would comprise 52.9%, the agency said
  - By Crystal Hsu / Staff reporter
 Taiwan’s population is projected to shrink by almost half over the next five decades, intensifying labor shortages and placing a growing drag on economic growth as the technology-intensive economy confronts a rapidly aging workforce. The population is expected to fall to 12.15 million by 2075, a 48 percent decline from this year, National Development Council projections released yesterday showed. The decline would fundamentally alter Taiwan’s workforce. From 2037, more than half of the working-age population is projected to be aged between 45 and 64, signaling the end of an era when the economy could rely on a relatively large labor force. Children climb on playground equipment at a park in Taipei yesterday.Photo: CNA The shift threatens to challenge Taiwan’s growth model, which depends on a broad manufacturing workforce and a growing supply of highly skilled workers to support its semiconductor and artificial intelligence industries. A shrinking pool of workers could make recruitment increasingly difficult, while a growing elderly population would add pressure on social spending and public finances. The projections also point to a deeper demographic problem — Taiwan is not only losing its population, but failing to replenish it, the council said. It lowered its long-term fertility assumptions after the fertility rate fell to a record low 0.695 last year, significantly below previous estimates. The number of women aged 20 to 49 has declined since peaking in 2005, while the proportion of married women in that age group has also fallen. The shrinking pool of potential mothers is making a sustained recovery in births increasingly difficult, it said. Taiwan’s population is projected to fall below 20 million in 2045, dropping to 19.98 million. People aged 65 or older are expected to account for 37 percent of the population, while the working-age population would shrink to 57.9 percent and children to just 5.2 percent, the council said. By 2075, the imbalance would be even more pronounced, with older people projected to comprise 52.9 percent of the population, working-age people 42.3 percent and children 4.8 percent, it said. The dependency ratio — the number of children and elderly people relative to those of working age — is projected to rise from 55.2 dependents for every 100 working-age people to 136.6 by 2075, the council said. The potential support ratio is expected to fall below one, suggesting less than one working-age person for every person aged 65 or older, it said. The government is preparing the economy for a permanently smaller workforce. It has established a population strategy task force, and in May launched 18 measures covering childbirth support, childcare, education, workplace policies and housing. Additional policy packages would target elderly people, talent development across all age groups and the recruitment of overseas talent, the council said. For businesses, the implications extend beyond hiring. Companies are likely to face greater pressure to raise labor force participation among elderly people, attract workers from overseas, and accelerate automation and productivity gains.

deduped_items.title: CEC approves nuclear referendum, rejects other two
deduped_items.body_text:
- 
            CEC approves nuclear referendum, rejects other twoCONDEMNED: The KMT slammed the rejections, saying the CEC decided on behalf of 23 million people, while the TPP said it brought shame to Taiwan’s democratic system
  - By Hsu Yung-ching / Staff reporter
 The Central Election Commission (CEC) yesterday announced it has approved holding a referendum on nuclear power, but rejected proposals on caning and traffic fines. The Legislative Yuan on Aug. 14 approved three referendums: introducing caning as a criminal punishment, abolishing the government’s nuclear-free homeland policy and using traffic fines to improve road safety. The commission met for more than two and a half hours, and ruled that the referendum on caning did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act (公民投票法), CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said. Central Election Commission Chairman Michael You speaks at a news conference in Taipei yesterday.Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times The caning proposal, put forward by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), seeks to introduce caning as a punishment for sexual assault, crimes against children, large-scale fraud and aggravated fraud. However, caning or similar forms of corporal punishment are not recognized under Taiwan’s criminal justice system, You said. The CEC therefore determined that the proposal amounted to creating new legislative principles, and was not a referendum on the initiation or repeal of a major policy, as defined by the act, he added. The proposal involves using state power to inflict physical pain on prisoners and is considered by many countries to be cruel, inhuman and a violation of human dignity, he said. That would contravene the Act Governing Execution of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (公民與政治權利國際公約及經濟社會文化權利國際公約施行法), which states that no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, he added. Of the eight CEC members, seven voted that the caning proposal did not qualify as a referendum, said You, who chaired the meeting, adding that he did not cast a vote. Regarding the Taiwan People’s Party’s (TPP) proposed referendum on earmarking traffic fines exclusively for road-related purposes, four commission members found that it did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said. The commission held three rounds of voting, with the same 4-3 split each time, he added. As for the proposal to repeal Taiwan’s nuclear-free homeland policy, six CEC members supported the referendum, with one abstention, You said. The CEC ruled that the proposal meets the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said, adding that the referendum vote would be held on Nov. 28, alongside the local elections. The KMT caucus condemned the CEC’s decision to reject the two proposals, saying that referendums exist to give people a direct say when a country faces major disputes over public policy. “Yet what has happened now is that whether people want to vote no longer matters, and neither does whether the Legislative Yuan approves the proposal,” it said. “Instead the CEC has decided on behalf of 23 million people: ‘You are not entitled to answer this question.’” “Is this direct democracy, or the direct confiscation of democracy?” it asked. The TPP slammed You, saying he had claimed that “referendums submitted by the Legislative Yuan should be approved in principle and rejected only as an exception.” “Yet he has now turned that exception into a pretext for arbitrarily expanding his powers, abandoning his principles as an academic, enabling the ruling party to flout the law and obstructing the public’s right to initiate referendums,” it said. “Such actions have brought shame on Taiwan’s democratic constitutional system.” Additional reporting by Lin Hsin-han

deduped_items.title: Prosecutors indict nine in Dr Shine hidden camera case
deduped_items.body_text:
- 
            Prosecutors indict nine in Dr Shine hidden camera case
  - By Wang Ting-chuan and Jake Chung / Staff reporter, with staff writer
 Prosecutors yesterday indicted nine people for allegedly installing hidden surveillance cameras in eight Dr Shine (光澤) clinics in Taipei and New Taipei City, and secretly recording more than 300 patients — including four minors — while they were exposed. Investigations into other branches allegedly involved in the case are still ongoing. The New Taipei City District Prosecutors’ Office is seeking a prison term of 16 years for Dr Shine group operations manager Chen Chih-min (陳志敏), 14 years for company information department head Tang Yung-chieh (唐詠傑) and seven years for surveillance camera supplier Chang Chao-ming (張朝銘). A branch of the Dr Shine cosmetics chain is pictured in New Taipei City in an undated photograph.Photo: Hsu Sheng-lun, Taipei Times They also proposed seven years for Dr Shine employee Chiang Chin-wei (江勁緯) and unspecified prison terms for five other employees embroiled in the case. Chen and Tang had abused clients’ trust, shown no remorse, offered no public apology and attempted to deceive police into believing that the devices had been removed years earlier, so they should receive severe sentences, the prosecutors’ office said in the indictment. Prosecutors also called on Dr Shine owner Wang Chao-huei (王朝輝) to return to Taiwan to face investigation over the scandal. Wang traveled to China before the incident came to light, but has allegedly shown no sign of willingly returning to Taiwan, even after a wanted notice was issued for him. Chen and Tang allegedly installed surveillance cameras disguised as smoke detectors or sensor-activated lighting at two Dr Shine clinics in New Taipei City’s Banciao District (板橋); and one each in Sanxia District (三峽), Sanchong District (三重) and Sinjhuang District (新莊), prosecutors said. They installed the same devices at clinics in Taipei’s Guting District (古亭), Daan District (大安) and Songshan District (松山), they added. Tang allegedly created a Line group that included Chen and others, and used it to direct efforts to remove surveillance cameras from all branches between May 5 and May 8, prosecutors said. The installation of cameras allegedly gave Chen and Tang access to private moments when patients were exposed, severely infringing on people’s constitutionally guaranteed rights to privacy and self-determination, prosecutors added.

‘Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang,’ ‘Sister Stella L’ to lead PFIM 2026 screenings
With the theme “Pelikula: Ginintuang Ikalawa,” this year’s celebration of the Philippine Film Industry Month (PFIM) will feature screenings of digitally restored classics including Lino Brocka’s “Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang” and Mike de Leon’s “Sister Stella L,” among others.
The Film Development Council of the Philippines (FDCP) announced PFIM’s monthlong activities that celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Second Golden Age of Philippine Cinema.
The screening of “Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang” will kick off the celebration at the Red Carpet Cinema, Shangri-La Plaza on Sept. 4, along with the announcement of the Philippines’ entry to the 2027 Oscars Best International Feature Film category.
Other digitally restored classics — including de Leon’s “Itim,” Brocka’s “Insiang,” Mario O’Hara’s “Tatlong Taong Walang Diyos,” Lupita Aquino-Kashiwahara’s “Minsa’y Isang Gamu-Gamo,” Eddie Romero’s “Ganito Kami Noon… Paano Kayo Ngayon?” and Ishmael Bernal’s “Nunal sa Tubig” — will be showcased throughout the month at FDCP Cinematheque Centres nationwide.
The audiences will also be taken further back in time with the “SineUna: Cinematic Action Before the War,” which will feature Eduardo de Castro’s “Zamboanga,” Carlos Vander Tolosa’s “Giliw Ko,” Vicente Salumbide’s “Ibong Adarna” and Octavio Silos’ “Tunay na Ina” and “Pakiusap.”
Meanwhile, the newly digitally-restored “Sister Stella L” will have its grand homecoming on Sept. 20 at the Metropolitan Theater as part of the “Mga Hiyas ng Sineng Pilipino,” which is co-presented by the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA).
READ: FDCP sets 1st Nat’l Cinema Day in Sept. with aim to bring audiences back to theaters
Other key PFIM 2026 events include the “Reel to Real: Pelikula at Panayam,” which will spotlight Brocka’s “Jaguar”; the Director’s Series, which will feature Jeffrey Jeturian’s “Tuhog” and “Kubrador”; the world premiere of Mike Alcazaren’s documentary film “Kodomo-tachi: Children of the War” on Sept. 17; the inaugural edition of the PFIM Short Film Competition; Sine Kabataan 2026; and the return of the Film Education Convention (FilmEc).
The PFIM 2026 will conclude with a closing ceremony on Sept. 30. /ra

deduped_items.title: Japan probes 39kg of bread dumped in national park
deduped_items.summary: A total of 39kg (85 lbs) of bread was recently dumped along a roadside in a national park in western Japan, prompting police to investigate who discarded it and why. The loaves were left near crash barriers in Daisen-Oki National Park in Tottori Prefecture between August 14 and 20. The incident has prompted the spread of fake images and videos attempting to link the dumping to a sharp increase in bear encounters in Japan over the past year. “When I first heard of the reports, my head was full of
deduped_items.body_text:
Japan probes 39kg of bread dumped in national park
The bread was initially believed to have been used as bait for cameras live streaming images of animals, but no such equipment was found
A total of 39kg (85 lbs) of bread was recently dumped along a roadside in a national park in western Japan, prompting police to investigate who discarded it and why.
The loaves were left near crash barriers in Daisen-Oki National Park in Tottori Prefecture between August 14 and 20. The incident has prompted the spread of fake images and videos attempting to link the dumping to a sharp increase in bear encounters in Japan over the past year.
“When I first heard of the reports, my head was full of question marks,” said Koji Iwaihara, director of the Natural Parks Foundation’s Tottori branch.
The bread was initially believed to have been used as bait for cameras live streaming images of animals, but no such equipment was found. The foundation later came to believe the bread had been left to feed animals after 1.3kg of chicken was found in the same area.
Bread was also found scattered around the prefecture’s Hakuto coast, but the brand appears to be different from that found in the national park. Neither the bread nor the chicken was poisoned.

deduped_items.title: Scientists probe if herpes virus is killing sardines off South Africa
deduped_items.summary: Scientists in South Africa are investigating why masses of sardines have washed up dead or dying along parts of the country’s west and south coast – and if a herpes virus detected in the fish is responsible. The mass mortality of sardines this month has so far stumped the country’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, though scientists have come to at least one conclusion: it is the first time that the virus in question – pilchard herpesvirus, or PHV – has been identified in...
deduped_items.body_text:
Scientists probe if herpes virus is killing sardines off South Africa
Pilchard herpesvirus is a fish virus and poses no known risk to human health
Scientists in South Africa are investigating why masses of sardines have washed up dead or dying along parts of the country’s west and south coast – and if a herpes virus detected in the fish is responsible.
The mass mortality of sardines this month has so far stumped the country’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, though scientists have come to at least one conclusion: it is the first time that the virus in question – pilchard herpesvirus, or PHV – has been identified in sardines off South Africa.
PHV, which was linked to two mass sardine mortality events in Australia in the 1990s, can cause inflammation and thickening of sardines’ gills, which interferes with their oxygen uptake, according to the South African environment department.
Sardines and pilchards are the same type of fish, with sardines being the younger, smaller ones.
PHV is a fish virus and poses no known risk to human health, the department said, and its detection does not mean that healthy sardines caught commercially or canned sardine products are unsafe to eat.
Dozens of sardines taken from affected areas, some dead and some alive, are being examined by scientists at the South African Institute for Aquatic Biodiversity and a local university.

deduped_items.title: Statins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial shows
deduped_items.summary: Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older peopleTaking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high chol
deduped_items.body_text:
Taking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.
Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having a major heart event such as a heart attack, stroke, or from requiring heart surgery.
People who have already had a major heart event are also commonly prescribed the drugs, regardless of their age.
What doctors did not know was whether it was safe to prescribe a daily statin to people aged 70 and over who were healthy overall, having never experienced a heart attack, stroke or heart surgery, and whether doing so could prevent these cardiac events.
A co-author of the study, Adjunct Prof Mark Nelson with the Monash University school of public health and preventive medicine, said it was an important piece of missing information, because the biggest risk of major heart-related events “is increasing age”.
“Our society is ageing, and therefore the burden of disease is increasing, making it important to improve our ability to prevent disease in this group,” he said. “So we needed the evidence for this group to see if prescribing statins as a prevention measure works.”
But Nelson said older adults were often overlooked in early statin research because 40 years ago, heart disease was most common in middle-aged populations especially if they smoked, leading public health efforts to focus on preventing premature deaths in that group. Elderly populations may also be sick and on other medications, making trialling drugs risky, he said.
To address the gap, Monash researchers analysed the cardiovascular outcomes of almost 10,000 study participants over the age of 70 who were given either a daily statin or a placebo, in a scientifically-robust type of study known as a randomised control trial. The participants were enrolled with the help of almost 3,400 GPs across Australia.
The researchers excluded people who had a condition that might make taking a statin unsafe, if they were not living independently, or if they already needed the drug because they had suffered a heart attack.
The decade-long study found the medication decreased the risk of a first major cardiovascular event by 30% for those aged over 70.
In real terms, this means one major cardiac event such as a heart attack, stroke, or heart surgery could be prevented for every 37 older adults treated with daily statins over almost six years.
Prof James Chong, a cardiologist at Sydney’s Westmead hospital, said if the research “leads to increased statin use globally, the absolute reduction of (heart-related) events can be significant”.
“One of the major changes that may result, in my opinion, is more elderly patients having confidence to take long term statins,” he said.
“However, one thing we have to keep in mind is it was an almost exclusively white population with the mean age around 75 years of age, so the results may not be as generalisable globally without further supporting evidence.”
The findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine on Saturday and presented concurrently at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Germany.
Lead researcher on the paper, Adjunct Prof Sophia Zoungas, said: “What we hope to see, now that we have provided such strong evidence, are updated treatment guidelines to help clinicians make use of this new finding.”
Older patients should have a conversation with their GP about whether statins are appropriate to help them stay healthy, the researchers said.
Prof Tom Marwick, a cardiologist at Hobart’s Royal hospital, said there had been a lot of misinformation about statins increasing the risk of dementia, making some older people reluctant to take the drugs.

deduped_items.title: Statins can safely cut risk of heart attacks or strokes in healthy people aged over 70, world-first clinical trial shows
deduped_items.summary: Australian-led trial finds low risk of side effects from common cholesterol-lowering medication for otherwise healthy older peopleTaking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high chol
deduped_items.body_text:
Taking a common cholesterol-lowering medication can reduce the risk of a heart attack or stroke for people aged over 70, with a low risk of serious side effects, a world-first clinical trial led by Australian researchers has found.
Statins are already commonly prescribed to people under the age of 75 who meet certain risk criteria, such as having diabetes and high cholesterol, to prevent them from having a major heart event such as a heart attack, stroke, or from requiring heart surgery.
People who have already had a major heart event are also commonly prescribed the drugs, regardless of their age.
What doctors did not know was whether it was safe to prescribe a daily statin to people aged 70 and over who were healthy overall, having never experienced a heart attack, stroke or heart surgery, and whether doing so could prevent these cardiac events.
A co-author of the study, Adjunct Prof Mark Nelson with the Monash University school of public health and preventive medicine, said it was an important piece of missing information, because the biggest risk of major heart-related events “is increasing age”.
“Our society is ageing, and therefore the burden of disease is increasing, making it important to improve our ability to prevent disease in this group,” he said. “So we needed the evidence for this group to see if prescribing statins as a prevention measure works.”
But Nelson said older adults were often overlooked in early statin research because 40 years ago, heart disease was most common in middle-aged populations especially if they smoked, leading public health efforts to focus on preventing premature deaths in that group. Elderly populations may also be sick and on other medications, making trialling drugs risky, he said.
To address the gap, Monash researchers analysed the cardiovascular outcomes of almost 10,000 study participants over the age of 70 who were given either a daily statin or a placebo, in a scientifically-robust type of study known as a randomised control trial. The participants were enrolled with the help of almost 3,400 GPs across Australia.
The researchers excluded people who had a condition that might make taking a statin unsafe, if they were not living independently, or if they already needed the drug because they had suffered a heart attack.
The decade-long study found the medication decreased the risk of a first major cardiovascular event by 30% for those aged over 70.
In real terms, this means one major cardiac event such as a heart attack, stroke, or heart surgery could be prevented for every 37 older adults treated with daily statins over almost six years.
Prof James Chong, a cardiologist at Sydney’s Westmead hospital, said if the research “leads to increased statin use globally, the absolute reduction of (heart-related) events can be significant”.
“One of the major changes that may result, in my opinion, is more elderly patients having confidence to take long term statins,” he said.
“However, one thing we have to keep in mind is it was an almost exclusively white population with the mean age around 75 years of age, so the results may not be as generalisable globally without further supporting evidence.”
The findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine on Saturday and presented concurrently at the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Germany.
Lead researcher on the paper, Adjunct Prof Sophia Zoungas, said: “What we hope to see, now that we have provided such strong evidence, are updated treatment guidelines to help clinicians make use of this new finding.”
Older patients should have a conversation with their GP about whether statins are appropriate to help them stay healthy, the researchers said.
Prof Tom Marwick, a cardiologist at Hobart’s Royal hospital, said there had been a lot of misinformation about statins increasing the risk of dementia, making some older people reluctant to take the drugs.

deduped_items.title: One Nation wants to restrict migration. A town in Barnaby Joyce's electorate welcomes it – video
deduped_items.summary: Since 2018, the New South Wales city of Armidale has been a designated site for resettling refugees. It's a town that sits within the electorate of Barnaby Joyce. While Joyce was a key voice supporting Armidale's establishment as a refugee resettlement site, he's since defected from the Nationals to One Nation, a party which wants to ban all migrants who don't speak English. Guardian Australia's community affairs reporter Adeshola Ore travels to Armidale to speak with Joyce and community members

deduped_items.title: Seven First Nations Australians tell us their worries and hopes for future generations – video
deduped_items.summary: East Arnhem Land is one of the last strongholds of Aboriginal culture in Australia, home to the Yolngu people who maintain one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. The land is fully owned and managed by traditional owners under inalienable Aboriginal freehold title, which means it can never be bought or sold. Each year the Yolngu host the Garma festival, Australia's largest Indigenous political and cultural gathering, which brings together First Nations leaders from around the country. Gu

deduped_items.title: What the CIA director’s mystery trip to Moscow says about Putin's next move
deduped_items.summary: An unannounced but highly visible flight to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe aboard a U.S. Air Force transport plane this week has ignited a fierce debate over Vladimir Putin’s next military move. With Russia’s volunteer recruitment drying up and its economy straining under the weight of 1.4 million casualties, intelligence briefs suggest Putin is preparing a massive, unpopular mobilization of 600,000 new troops.

deduped_items.title: «Chambres noires»: entre l’ombre et la lumière
deduped_items.summary: Suivant les traces de la photographe américaine Vivian Maier, Dominique Fortier raconte son histoire «la plus fragile».
deduped_items.body_text:
En 2007, dans une vente aux enchères de Chicago, John Maloof, un jeune Américain, a fait l’acquisition un peu à l’aveugle de boîtes pleines de négatifs, de rouleaux de pellicule jamais développés, de bobines de film et d’impressions photographiques. Un univers englouti reprenait vie.
Cette photographe de rue amatrice, une parfaite inconnue qui a travaillé pendant 40 ans comme nounou, s’appelait Vivian Maier (1926-2009). L’existence de cette femme, révélée au monde grâce au fascinant documentaire réalisé par John Maloof et Charlie Siskel en 2013, Finding Vivian Maier (À la recherche de Vivian Maier), se résume aujourd’hui à peu de choses, sinon aux dizaines de milliers de photographies qu’elle a prises — beaucoup d’autoportraits, Rolleiflex autour du cou —, dont certaines sont exposées aujourd’hui dans plusieurs musées dans le monde.
Une sorte de mystère, un mythe, dont Dominique Fortier s’intéresse à l’« œuvre fantôme, inachevée et sauvage » dans Chambres noires, son onzième titre en solo. Un livre dans lequel elle mêle des jalons de l’histoire de la photographie, des hypothèses sur la vie de Vivian Maier ainsi que des éléments pour elle plus intimes, qui tourne autour du motif de la révélation — qui consiste, en photographie argentique, à rendre visible l’image latente et invisible enregistrée sur le film ou le papier lors de l’exposition à la lumière.
                                
                    « L’œil est toujours entraîné vers on ne sait pas quoi. C’est comme s’il voulait s’échapper du cadre. »
Dominique Fortier
Photo: Valérian Mazataud Le Devoir
Écrivaine discrète, Dominique Fortier semble s’y dévoiler un peu plus qu’à l’habitude, évoquant en parallèle de la vie de Vivian Maier l’existence de sa sœur aînée décédée lorsqu’elle avait 3 ans. Un « petit fantôme » qui l’accompagne depuis et dont elle n’a conservé aucun souvenir. Sinon des photos de famille charcutées, une tristesse diffuse, un silence qui pèse. La présence d’une absence. « Les secrets, les silences. Tous ces blancs qui font aussi les livres. »
Une histoire, écrit l’autrice d’Au péril de la mer (Alto, 2015, Prix littéraire du Gouverneur général), née à Québec en 1972, qui est pour elle « la plus personnelle et la plus fragile ». Et c’est armée de sa pudeur coutumière qu’elle développe dans Chambres noires son intérêt pour les fantômes.
« Son œuvre est caractérisée par une chose que j’appellerais l’esthétique du choc, de la collision. Elle fonctionne en mettant ensemble des choses qui ne devraient pas se rencontrer », fait remarquer Dominique Fortier depuis sa maison du Maine, en cette fin du mois d’août qui marque à regret le début du compte à rebours des jours qu’il lui reste avant de rentrer à Montréal. Dans les photos de Vivian Maier, témoin autant d’une époque que d’un lieu, « l’œil est toujours entraîné vers on ne sait pas quoi. C’est comme s’il voulait s’échapper du cadre ». Son regard lui semble aussi porter un mélange de tendresse et de quelque chose d’implacable.
La petite-fille d’Emily Dickinson
Si l’écrivaine ne se souvient pas de sa première rencontre avec Vivian Maier et avec son œuvre, elle a l’impression que c’est comme si elles avaient toujours été là. Mais elle se souvient que le 11 août 2025, en rentrant à Montréal après avoir passé l’été au bord de la mer, Dominique Fortier a aperçu dans la vitrine d’une maison de la presse la couverture d’un magazine, un numéro spécial, consacré à la photographe américaine. « Je ne sais pas ce que ça a provoqué chez moi, mais c’était suffisamment fort pour que j’achète la revue, que je rentre chez nous, que je la pose à côté de moi, puis que je me mette à écrire tout de suite. Il y avait quelque chose comme un appel. » Ces photos lui parlaient, elles ont réveillé en elle quelque chose.
C’était un peu, relate-t-elle, comme si Vivian Maier lui disait : « Raconte ma vie. » Alors que c’était peut-être elle, en réalité, qui aidait Dominique Fortier à raconter la sienne. Quelques mois plus tard, en novemb

deduped_items.title: Limo, una muestra que lleva el arte del Norte argentino a Recoleta
deduped_items.summary: Limo nació del encuentro entre Otto Galería, de Tilcara, Uncu y el coleccionista y curador Joaquín Rodríguez. La exposición reúne textiles, fotografías, dibujos, cerámicas y objetos atravesados por las relaciones entre territorio, cultura e identidad. Entre los artistas participantes se encuentran Marcelo Abud, Florencia Blanco, Fidela Flores, Victoria Pastrana y Ariel Pascuali.

Mujer de Atlanta recibe 16 años de prisión por fraude masivo contra Amazon: 'Casi 10 millones de dólares en tan solo unos meses'
Según la investigación, el caso ocurrió desde un almacén en Georgia. Le imputaron cargos por lavado de dinero y falsificación de documentos.
El pasado miércoles 26 de agosto, una mujer en Atlanta identificada como Brittany Hudson fue condenada a más de 16 años de prisión tras ser declarada culpable de organizar un fraude millonario contra Amazon.
De acuerdo con el comunicado oficial de la Fiscalía Federal de Estados Unidos para el Distrito Norte de Georgia, la estafa alcanzó los "10 millones de dólares en tan solo unos meses".
¿Cómo se dio el fraude millonario contra Amazon?
De acuerdo con los funcionarios de los Estados Unidos, "Hudson era dueña de un negocio que contrataba con Amazon y tenía una relación con Kayricka Wortham, quien trabajaba como gerente de operaciones en el almacén de la empresa en Smyrna, Georgia".
El expediente señala que entre enero y junio de 2022, la pareja engañó a algunos trabajadores para que agregaran vendedores falsos al sistema de la compañía, dijeron las autoridades.
Seguido de esto, enviaron facturas falsificadas que mostraban que los falsos vendedores habían proporcionado a Amazon varios bienes y servicios.
De modo que, por el cargo que poseía Wortham en la empresa, pudo aprobar sin preocupación alguna las facturas, transfiriendo 9,4 millones de dólares a cuentas bancarias que la pareja y otros coconspiradores poseían.
Parte del dinero obtenido mediante el fraude terminó convertido en bienes de alto valor. Según CBS News Atlanta, entre las compras realizadas están:
Una casa de casi 1 millón de dólares en Smyrna.
Un Lamborghini Urus 2019.
Un Dodge Durango 2021.
Un Tesla Model X 2022.
Un Porsche Panamera 2018.
Una motocicleta Kawasaki ZX636.
La acusación fue emitida en septiembre de 2022
Según informes de la Oficina del Fiscal del Distrito Norte de Georgia, en septiembre de 2022, las autoridades federales descubrieron el fraude y acusaron formalmente a la pareja.

Mujer de Atlanta recibe 16 años de prisión por fraude masivo contra Amazon: 'Casi 10 millones de dólares en tan solo unos meses'
Según la investigación, el caso ocurrió desde un almacén en Georgia. Le imputaron cargos por lavado de dinero y falsificación de documentos.
El pasado miércoles 26 de agosto, una mujer en Atlanta identificada como Brittany Hudson fue condenada a más de 16 años de prisión tras ser declarada culpable de organizar un fraude millonario contra Amazon.
De acuerdo con el comunicado oficial de la Fiscalía Federal de Estados Unidos para el Distrito Norte de Georgia, la estafa alcanzó los "10 millones de dólares en tan solo unos meses".
¿Cómo se dio el fraude millonario contra Amazon?
De acuerdo con los funcionarios de los Estados Unidos, "Hudson era dueña de un negocio que contrataba con Amazon y tenía una relación con Kayricka Wortham, quien trabajaba como gerente de operaciones en el almacén de la empresa en Smyrna, Georgia".
El expediente señala que entre enero y junio de 2022, la pareja engañó a algunos trabajadores para que agregaran vendedores falsos al sistema de la compañía, dijeron las autoridades.
Seguido de esto, enviaron facturas falsificadas que mostraban que los falsos vendedores habían proporcionado a Amazon varios bienes y servicios.
De modo que, por el cargo que poseía Wortham en la empresa, pudo aprobar sin preocupación alguna las facturas, transfiriendo 9,4 millones de dólares a cuentas bancarias que la pareja y otros coconspiradores poseían.
Parte del dinero obtenido mediante el fraude terminó convertido en bienes de alto valor. Según CBS News Atlanta, entre las compras realizadas están:
Una casa de casi 1 millón de dólares en Smyrna.
Un Lamborghini Urus 2019.
Un Dodge Durango 2021.
Un Tesla Model X 2022.
Un Porsche Panamera 2018.
Una motocicleta Kawasaki ZX636.
La acusación fue emitida en septiembre de 2022

“It’s Very Likely That a Different Party System Will Emerge in Venezuela”
Prof. Guillermo Aveledo Coll discusses the unfolding negotiations, the future of political parties, and the lessons Rómulo Betancourt might offer Machado
The trajectory of the political transition that many Venezuelans await since January 3 seems to have been clarifying over the past few weeks. The first expected milestone is the reform of the Supreme Court of Justice, although it remains to be seen how many of the new magistrates will be independent and how many tied to factions of the chavista elite. The expectation is that, before the end of the year, the agenda will include a new board of rectors for the CNE and the long-awaited electoral calendar. In Panama, María Corina Machado had opened to negotiating these matters directly with Delcy Rodríguez, but the United States decided to manage the institutional opening through a small group of opposition figures, former lawmakers from Primero Justicia and Voluntad Popular in the 2015 National Assembly. The discomfort of Machado and her inner circle with this decision is no secret. The opposition leader has stated that she does not intend to stand in the way. Individuals linked to her team and party have raised doubts about the negotiation’s initial legitimacy and early progress, while other longtime opposition figures have welcomed the recent releases of political prisoners and the roadmap the US has outlined.
At Caracas Chronicles, we sat down to talk with Guillermo Aveledo Coll, a political scientist, expert in Venezuelan political history, and researcher of the ideas that have shaped its parties and conflicts. Aveledo views the unfolding dialogue favorably. He believes general elections must take place in Venezuela as soon as possible, though not without first tying up loose ends related to the broad recognition of any electoral process and the stability of future governments. He also discussed the dynamics that could emerge among political parties amid a transition, both within the anti-chavista camp and inside the chavista movement. Much like Marco Rubio in January, he made reference to the Spanish Transition. Finally, he reflected on our last transition to democracy (1958–1968) and how Rómulo Betancourt and Acción Democrática adapted to move forward in the face of adversity.
Recently, María Corina Machado used a term typical in transition frameworks. She said that the transition to democracy cannot be an elite pact made behind the people’s backs and without a popular mandate. Does the agenda unfolding between a commission of the Delcy government and the Delegated Commission of the old 2015 National Assembly fall into the category of an elite pact? You have been a defender of the legacy of the Puntofijo Pact. Is an elite pact problematic in these particular circumstances?
What we are seeing, which points embryonically toward an elite agreement, will have to be filtered through the will of the population, because the ultimate source of legitimacy in a democratic republic passes through it. The Puntofijo Pact was a concrete agreement on political rules among parties. However, had those parties lacked inherent legitimacy and a firm foothold, those rules might have overwhelmed them. In those elections, an independent candidate backed by one of the historic parties, Rear Admiral Wolfgang Larrazábal, obtained a very high percentage of the vote and came in second. So it could very well have been something that surpassed them, that swallowed them up.
Venezuela will need elections. It also needs the freedoms and guarantees for those elections to take place. Not because winning them without those guarantees is impossible, but because the opposition’s victories haven’t been recognized without them, while a government win leaves reasonable doubts regarding legitimacy. Prof. Guillermo Aveledo Coll discusses the unfolding negotiations, the future of political parties, and the lessons Rómulo Betancourt might offer Machado
The trajectory of the political transition that many Venezuelans await since January 3 seems to have been clarifying over the past few weeks. The first expected milestone is the reform of the Supreme Court of Justice, although it remains to be seen how many of the new magistrates will be independent and how many tied to factions of the chavista elite. The expectation is that, before the end of the year, the agenda will include a new board of rectors for the CNE and the long-awaited electoral calendar. In Panama, María Corina Machado had opened to negotiating these matters directly with Delcy Rodríguez, but the United States decided to manage the institutional opening through a small group of opposition figures, former lawmakers from Primero Justicia and Voluntad Popular in the 2015 National Assembly. The discomfort of Machado and her inner circle with this decision is no secret. The opposition leader has stated that she does not intend to stand in the way. Individuals linked to her team and party have raised doubts about the negotiation’s initial legitimacy and early progress, while other longtime opposition figures have welcomed the recent releases of political prisoners and the roadmap the US has outlined.
At Caracas Chronicles, we sat down to talk with Guillermo Aveledo Coll, a political scientist, expert in Venezuelan political history, and researcher of the ideas that have shaped its parties and conflicts. Aveledo views the unfolding dialogue favorably. He believes general elections must take place in Venezuela as soon as possible, though not without first tying up loose ends related to the broad recognition of any electoral process and the stability of future governments. He also discussed the dynamics that could emerge among political parties amid a transition, both within the anti-chavista camp and inside the chavista movement. Much like Marco Rubio in January, he made reference to the Spanish Transition. Finally, he reflected on our last transition to democracy (1958–1968) and how Rómulo Betancourt and Acción Democrática adapted to move forward in the face of adversity.
Recently, María Corina Machado used a term typical in transition frameworks. She said that the transition to democracy cannot be an elite pact made behind the people’s backs and without a popular mandate. Does the agenda unfolding between a commission of the Delcy government and the Delegated Commission of the old 2015 National Assembly fall into the category of an elite pact? You have been a defender of the legacy of the Puntofijo Pact. Is an elite pact problematic in these particular circumstances?
What we are seeing, which points embryonically toward an elite agreement, will have to be filtered through the will of the population, because the ultimate source of legitimacy in a democratic republic passes through it. The Puntofijo Pact was a concrete agreement on political rules among parties. However, had those parties lacked inherent legitimacy and a firm foothold, those rules might have overwhelmed them. In those elections, an independent candidate backed by one of the historic parties, Rear Admiral Wolfgang Larrazábal, obtained a very high percentage of the vote and came in second. So it could very well have been something that surpassed them, that swallowed them up.
Venezuela will need elections. It also needs the freedoms and guarantees for those elections to take place. Not because winning them without those guarantees is impossible, but because the opposition’s victories haven’t been recognized without them, while a government win leaves reasonable doubts regarding legitimacy. deduped_items.title: For Tibetans, China’s ethnic minorities law is assimilation dressed up as ‘unity’
deduped_items.summary: On 1 July 2026, China’s National People’s Congress enacted the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, a 65-article statute passed in March by a near-unanimous vote. Beijing presents it as a modernising measure meant to bind the country’s 56 officially recognised ethnic groups into what officials call ‘a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation’. deduped_items.title: Fuel subsidy debate: Between economic reform and political expediency, By Ehi Braimah
deduped_items.summary: My view is that Nigeria does not need a return to an inefficient subsidy regime merely because petrol is expensive, neither does it need to worship the doctrine of subsidy removal while citizens are pushed deeper into poverty. What we need is affordable energy, accountable government and an economy that converts its enormous natural resource […] The post Fuel subsidy debate: Between economic reform and political expediency, By Ehi Braimah appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria.
deduped_items.body_text:
My view is that Nigeria does not need a return to an inefficient subsidy regime merely because petrol is expensive, neither does it need to worship the doctrine of subsidy removal while citizens are pushed deeper into poverty. What we need is affordable energy, accountable government and an economy that converts its enormous natural resource wealth into broad-based prosperity. The ultimate test of any economic policy is not whether economists approve of it, nor whether politicians can defend it.
Nigeria’s worsening cost-of-living crisis has turned petrol subsidy into one of the most politically sensitive issues ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The debate was reignited by former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), who has promised to restore petrol subsidy if elected president on 16 January, 2027. The date is the official presidential and National Assembly election date announced by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).
Atiku’s declaration has predictably generated political fireworks. The Presidency and All Progressives Congress (APC) voices have attacked the proposal, while some Nigerians, understandably exhausted by high prices, have welcomed the prospect of cheaper petrol. Other opposition figures, including Peter Obi, have questioned the wisdom of returning to the old subsidy regime.
At the heart of the argument is a deceptively simple question: Should an oil-producing country such as Nigeria subsidise petrol for its citizens? Atiku says ‘yes.’ His argument is that Nigeria is sufficiently endowed with crude oil resources to provide affordable energy to its people. He has also questioned what happened to the savings from subsidy removal and argued that Nigerians have not received commensurate benefits from the reform.
But is this serious economic policy or simply political speak ahead of an election? The answer may lie somewhere between the two.
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu set the tone for his administration’s economic policy on 29 May, 2023 when, immediately after taking the oath of office, he declared: “The fuel subsidy is gone.” The announcement was dramatic because it ended a policy that had existed for decades and had become deeply embedded in Nigeria’s political economy. Petrol prices immediately rose, with NNPC Limited adjusting pump prices within days to between ₦488 and ₦557 per litre in different parts of the country.
The reform was not isolated. Tinubu’s administration also unified the foreign exchange market, allowing the naira to depreciate substantially, while subsequently implementing other reforms affecting electricity pricing and public finances. The economic logic was compelling. Nigeria could no longer afford to spend enormous amounts of public money keeping petrol artificially cheap, particularly when the country was importing most of its refined petroleum products.
Nigeria’s economy was in bad shape due to decades of horrifying mismanagement. In 2022 alone, petrol subsidies cost Nigeria about $10 billion, according to Reuters. Nigeria had effectively been exporting crude oil, importing refined petrol and then borrowing or diverting scarce public resources to make imported petrol cheaper at the pump.
The subsidy was therefore not simply an energy policy – it was a major fiscal burden. But there was a problem. The economic argument for removing subsidy was stronger than the social protection programme that accompanied its removal. That is where the Tinubu administration has struggled.
For the average Nigerian, macroeconomic arguments about fiscal consolidation mean little when the price of petrol has risen several hundred per cent. Petrol that sold for about ₦175 per litre before the May 2023 announcement has, depending on location and market conditions, risen to around ₦1,250 to ₦1,300 or more. That represents an extraordinary increase in the cost of one of the most important commodities in the Nigerian economy.

My view is that Nigeria does not need a return to an inefficient subsidy regime merely because petrol is expensive, neither does it need to worship the doctrine of subsidy removal while citizens are pushed deeper into poverty. What we need is affordable energy, accountable government and an economy that converts its enormous natural resource wealth into broad-based prosperity. The ultimate test of any economic policy is not whether economists approve of it, nor whether politicians can defend it.
Nigeria’s worsening cost-of-living crisis has turned petrol subsidy into one of the most politically sensitive issues ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The debate was reignited by former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), who has promised to restore petrol subsidy if elected president on 16 January, 2027. The date is the official presidential and National Assembly election date announced by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).
Atiku’s declaration has predictably generated political fireworks. The Presidency and All Progressives Congress (APC) voices have attacked the proposal, while some Nigerians, understandably exhausted by high prices, have welcomed the prospect of cheaper petrol. Other opposition figures, including Peter Obi, have questioned the wisdom of returning to the old subsidy regime.
At the heart of the argument is a deceptively simple question: Should an oil-producing country such as Nigeria subsidise petrol for its citizens? Atiku says ‘yes.’ His argument is that Nigeria is sufficiently endowed with crude oil resources to provide affordable energy to its people. He has also questioned what happened to the savings from subsidy removal and argued that Nigerians have not received commensurate benefits from the reform.
But is this serious economic policy or simply political speak ahead of an election? The answer may lie somewhere between the two.
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu set the tone for his administration’s economic policy on 29 May, 2023 when, immediately after taking the oath of office, he declared: “The fuel subsidy is gone.” The announcement was dramatic because it ended a policy that had existed for decades and had become deeply embedded in Nigeria’s political economy. Petrol prices immediately rose, with NNPC Limited adjusting pump prices within days to between ₦488 and ₦557 per litre in different parts of the country.
The reform was not isolated. Tinubu’s administration also unified the foreign exchange market, allowing the naira to depreciate substantially, while subsequently implementing other reforms affecting electricity pricing and public finances. The economic logic was compelling. Nigeria could no longer afford to spend enormous amounts of public money keeping petrol artificially cheap, particularly when the country was importing most of its refined petroleum products.
Nigeria’s economy was in bad shape due to decades of horrifying mismanagement. In 2022 alone, petrol subsidies cost Nigeria about $10 billion, according to Reuters. Nigeria had effectively been exporting crude oil, importing refined petrol and then borrowing or diverting scarce public resources to make imported petrol cheaper at the pump.
The subsidy was therefore not simply an energy policy – it was a major fiscal burden. But there was a problem. The economic argument for removing subsidy was stronger than the social protection programme that accompanied its removal. That is where the Tinubu administration has struggled.
For the average Nigerian, macroeconomic arguments about fiscal consolidation mean little when the price of petrol has risen several hundred per cent. Petrol that sold for about ₦175 per litre before the May 2023 announcement has, depending on location and market conditions, risen to around ₦1,250 to ₦1,300 or more. That represents an extraordinary increase in the cost of one of the most important commodities in the Nigerian economy.

My view is that Nigeria does not need a return to an inefficient subsidy regime merely because petrol is expensive, neither does it need to worship the doctrine of subsidy removal while citizens are pushed deeper into poverty. What we need is affordable energy, accountable government and an economy that converts its enormous natural resource wealth into broad-based prosperity. The ultimate test of any economic policy is not whether economists approve of it, nor whether politicians can defend it.
Nigeria’s worsening cost-of-living crisis has turned petrol subsidy into one of the most politically sensitive issues ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The debate was reignited by former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), who has promised to restore petrol subsidy if elected president on 16 January, 2027. The date is the official presidential and National Assembly election date announced by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).
Atiku’s declaration has predictably generated political fireworks. The Presidency and All Progressives Congress (APC) voices have attacked the proposal, while some Nigerians, understandably exhausted by high prices, have welcomed the prospect of cheaper petrol. Other opposition figures, including Peter Obi, have questioned the wisdom of returning to the old subsidy regime.
At the heart of the argument is a deceptively simple question: Should an oil-producing country such as Nigeria subsidise petrol for its citizens? Atiku says ‘yes.’ His argument is that Nigeria is sufficiently endowed with crude oil resources to provide affordable energy to its people. He has also questioned what happened to the savings from subsidy removal and argued that Nigerians have not received commensurate benefits from the reform.
