Petrol prices immediately rose, with NNPC Limited adjusting pump prices within days to between ₦488 and ₦557 per litre in different parts of the country.
The reform was not isolated. Tinubu’s administration also unified the foreign exchange market, allowing the naira to depreciate substantially, while subsequently implementing other reforms affecting electricity pricing and public finances. The economic logic was compelling. Nigeria could no longer afford to spend enormous amounts of public money keeping petrol artificially cheap, particularly when the country was importing most of its refined petroleum products.
Nigeria’s economy was in bad shape due to decades of horrifying mismanagement. In 2022 alone, petrol subsidies cost Nigeria about $10 billion, according to Reuters. Nigeria had effectively been exporting crude oil, importing refined petrol and then borrowing or diverting scarce public resources to make imported petrol cheaper at the pump.
The subsidy was therefore not simply an energy policy – it was a major fiscal burden. But there was a problem. The economic argument for removing subsidy was stronger than the social protection programme that accompanied its removal. That is where the Tinubu administration has struggled.
For the average Nigerian, macroeconomic arguments about fiscal consolidation mean little when the price of petrol has risen several hundred per cent. Petrol that sold for about ₦175 per litre before the May 2023 announcement has, depending on location and market conditions, risen to around ₦1,250 to ₦1,300 or more. That represents an extraordinary increase in the cost of one of the most important commodities in the Nigerian economy.

deduped_items.title: “The Strategy of Terrorism”
deduped_items.summary: A quarter century before 9/11, an upsurge in global terrorism prompted the historian David Fromkin to examine its purpose and method. Terrorism was a strategy of the weak, Fromkin wrote in these pages, but modern technology had enabled it “to enter the political arena on a new scale.” And its surprising success seemed to be due, in large part, “to a miscomprehension of the strategy by its opponents.”

The unilateral announcement, posted to social media mere hours before the large-scale maneuvers involving 18,000 South Korean troops were set to launch, was justified by Washington […] The post The geopolitical imperative for a self-reliant South Korea appeared first on Asia Times.
deduped_items.body_text:
US President Donald Trump’s abrupt directive on August 16, 2026, to drastically scale back the joint “Ulchi Freedom Shield” (UFS) military exercises sent shockwaves across the Asia-Pacific geostrategic landscape.
The unilateral announcement, posted to social media mere hours before the large-scale maneuvers involving 18,000 South Korean troops were set to launch, was justified by Washington on grounds of cost efficiency, claims of a close personal rapport with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and executive frustration over South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s refusal to commit Seoul’s military to denuclearization operations against Iran.
This transactional and unilateral maneuver directly fractures the foundation of the US-led extended deterrence doctrine, which has served as the bedrock of stability on the Korean Peninsula for over seven decades.
When a nation’s security guarantees can be summarily revoked to accommodate Washington’s domestic political calculus, absolute reliance on the American defense umbrella ceases to be a protective asset. Instead, it becomes an existential vulnerability threatening national survival.
This new geostrategic reality compels South Korea to face an unavoidable historical crossroads. Discourse surrounding strategic autonomy has shifted radically: transitioning from a progressive academic debate into an urgent geopolitical imperative to safeguard national sovereignty against the erratic behavior of its principal ally.
The American dilemma
Washington’s unilateral decree demands an accelerated transfer of Wartime Operational Control (OPCON) to the South Korean military. Although evaluations for Full Operational Capability (FOC) are slated for completion in 2026, severe systemic gaps in intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) integration continue to cast a long shadow over Seoul.
Limitations in independent satellite monitoring to track North Korea’s highly mobile missile launchers and subterranean installations leave South Korea heavily dependent on Washington’s early-warning satellite network.
Without integrating AI-driven automated target recognition and rapidly deploying low-Earth-orbit micro-satellite constellations, assuming operational command risks creating critical tactical blind spots.
A parallel fragility haunts the paradox of South Korea’s defense industry (K-Defense). Despite remarkable global export surges, ranking 10th worldwide with a US$47.6 billion defense budget in 2024, South Korea’s military technology supply chain remains tightly tethered to US licensing.
A staggering 86% of South Korea’s total arms imports between 2020 and 2024 originated from the United States, while flagship platforms such as the KF-21 fighter jet and FA-50 light attack aircraft rely heavily on Washington-licensed engines and components.
International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) grant Washington effective veto power over South Korean arms exports; true industrial self-reliance thus requires aggressive domestic component substitution and supply chain diversification toward NATO partners.
At the strategic level, the conventional Three-Axis System and the ultra-heavy Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile reveal structural limitations when confronting a nuclear-armed adversary. The potential for preemptive escalation from Pyongyang makes conventional deterrence inadequate to guarantee absolute security.
While public opinion polls indicate 76% of South Koreans support developing an independent nuclear capability, backing among strategic experts hovers at just 30–40%, reflecting fears of international sanctions and economic isolation.
Consequently, the most pragmatic path for Seoul is pursuing “nuclear hedging”, drastically shortening its breakout time by developing civilian uranium enrichment and spent fuel reprocessing capabilities.

Israeli settlers surround another Palestinian home in Qusra, attack journalists in Jalud
Israeli settlers, backed by their military, have surrounded another Palestinian home in Qusra, south of Nablus, with at least four people trapped inside, Al Jazeera Arabic is reporting.
The settlers also reportedly set fire to nearby land, while efforts were underway to allow ambulances to evacuate a wounded person.
Qusra has faced relentless settler violence for weeks, with several homes in the Ras al-Ain area under siege since 9 August.
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, settlers attacked two elderly Palestinian women in Silwad while they were picking figs, Wafa news agency reported.
As per the report, the settlers also assaulted a Palestinian family and foreign journalists in Jalud, smashing the media crew’s vehicle.
The attacks come amid a surge in settler violence, with the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission reporting 2,256 attacks by Israeli soldiers and settlers against Palestinians and their property in July.

deduped_items.body_text:
How the military-industrial complex is waging war on the planet
The scale of the arms industry’s contribution to climate change is often minimised, avoided or ignored.
But preparations for war, and war itself, are killing the planet faster than practically any other single factor. The military-industrial complex causes more environmental damage than either the civilian aviation industry or the global shipping industry; in fact, its carbon footprint is close to both combined, according to a recent report.
It does so through both standard peacetime operations and the actual waging of war itself.
The best-known attempt to estimate the global military carbon footprint came in a 2022 study by researchers at Scientists for Global Responsibility and the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
They estimated it at about 5.5 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions, with a plausible range of 3.3-7 percent, larger than Russia’s national emissions - and that figure does not include the emissions generated by actual wars.

So why do the peacetime operations of the arms industry make such a huge contribution to climate change?
Firstly, modern armed forces depend heavily on oil. Fighter aircraft, bombers, helicopters, warships, tanks and military logistics fleets consume very large quantities of jet fuel and diesel. Military exercises and the worldwide movement of personnel and equipment add to this.
Nato itself now explicitly recognises military activities and installations as sources of greenhouse gases, and has even developed a methodology for measuring them.
Permanent footprint
Military infrastructure has a permanent footprint. Bases, airfields, naval facilities, radar installations, military housing and training grounds consume electricity and heating fuel, and require construction and maintenance.
Maintaining a worldwide network of military installations therefore generates emissions even when no war is taking place. Nato’s own accounting methodology explicitly includes military facilities and installations.
Secondly, weapons production - encompassing aircraft, ships, armoured vehicles, missiles, electronics, buildings and ammunition - has a large industrial footprint, requiring steel, aluminium, titanium, cement, chemicals and huge international supply chains.
Unless military production is radically de-escalated, it could burn the planet before it has a chance to bomb the planet
But that is just the start of it. Once soldiers begin using their weapons, the planet is among the first casualties. When fighting starts, aircraft fly far more missions, armoured vehicles operate continuously, ammunition has to be transported, ships deploy, and vast logistical systems move fuel, food, weapons and personnel. The carbon footprint of a military at war is thus substantially greater than its peacetime footprint.
The destruction of war magnifies the impacts on the environment. Attacks on oil refineries, fuel depots, factories, power stations and industrial facilities can release greenhouse gases directly and generate enormous fires.
Urban warfare can also burn buildings and vehicles. The Conflict and Environment Observatory consequently treats emissions generated by warfare as an additional category beyond the estimated 5.5 percent military footprint.
And even after the fighting stops, the costs to the environment continue to mount. Reconstruction can be exceptionally carbon-intensive. Destroying a city creates emissions during the attack, but rebuilding it requires huge quantities of cement, concrete, steel, glass and asphalt.
Cement and steel production are themselves major sources of carbon dioxide. A war can therefore create a second wave of emissions lasting many years after the fighting stops. The 5.5 percent estimate excludes post-conflict reconstruction.

deduped_items.body_text:
Israeli settlers surround another Palestinian home in Qusra, attack journalists in Jalud
Israeli settlers, backed by their military, have surrounded another Palestinian home in Qusra, south of Nablus, with at least four people trapped inside, Al Jazeera Arabic is reporting.
The settlers also reportedly set fire to nearby land, while efforts were underway to allow ambulances to evacuate a wounded person.
Qusra has faced relentless settler violence for weeks, with several homes in the Ras al-Ain area under siege since 9 August.
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, settlers attacked two elderly Palestinian women in Silwad while they were picking figs, Wafa news agency reported.
As per the report, the settlers also assaulted a Palestinian family and foreign journalists in Jalud, smashing the media crew’s vehicle.
The attacks come amid a surge in settler violence, with the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission reporting 2,256 attacks by Israeli soldiers and settlers against Palestinians and their property in July.

deduped_items.title: Africa’s Pension Funds Are Already Allowed to Invest at Home. They Don’t.
deduped_items.summary: Reformers keep asking governments to raise the ceilings on where domestic institutional capital can go. The ceilings are nowhere near being reached and one December in Ghana explains why. This article is published on African Arguments ahead of the African Development Summit which takes place on 18 September 2026. Nigeria’s pension regulator permits funds to hold up to 15 per cent of assets in private equity. Industry assets now stand above ₦31 trillion. Actual take-up sits far below the ceiling.

deduped_items.title: The geopolitical imperative for a self-reliant South Korea
deduped_items.summary: US President Donald Trump’s abrupt directive on August 16, 2026, to drastically scale back the joint “Ulchi Freedom Shield” (UFS) military exercises sent shockwaves across the Asia-Pacific geostrategic landscape. The unilateral announcement, posted to social media mere hours before the large-scale maneuvers involving 18,000 South Korean troops were set to launch, was justified by Washington […] The post The geopolitical imperative for a self-reliant South Korea appeared first on Asia Times.
deduped_items.body_text:
US President Donald Trump’s abrupt directive on August 16, 2026, to drastically scale back the joint “Ulchi Freedom Shield” (UFS) military exercises sent shockwaves across the Asia-Pacific geostrategic landscape.
The unilateral announcement, posted to social media mere hours before the large-scale maneuvers involving 18,000 South Korean troops were set to launch, was justified by Washington on grounds of cost efficiency, claims of a close personal rapport with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and executive frustration over South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s refusal to commit Seoul’s military to denuclearization operations against Iran.
This transactional and unilateral maneuver directly fractures the foundation of the US-led extended deterrence doctrine, which has served as the bedrock of stability on the Korean Peninsula for over seven decades.
When a nation’s security guarantees can be summarily revoked to accommodate Washington’s domestic political calculus, absolute reliance on the American defense umbrella ceases to be a protective asset. Instead, it becomes an existential vulnerability threatening national survival.
This new geostrategic reality compels South Korea to face an unavoidable historical crossroads. Discourse surrounding strategic autonomy has shifted radically: transitioning from a progressive academic debate into an urgent geopolitical imperative to safeguard national sovereignty against the erratic behavior of its principal ally.
The American dilemma
Washington’s unilateral decree demands an accelerated transfer of Wartime Operational Control (OPCON) to the South Korean military. Although evaluations for Full Operational Capability (FOC) are slated for completion in 2026, severe systemic gaps in intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) integration continue to cast a long shadow over Seoul.
Limitations in independent satellite monitoring to track North Korea’s highly mobile missile launchers and subterranean installations leave South Korea heavily dependent on Washington’s early-warning satellite network.
Without integrating AI-driven automated target recognition and rapidly deploying low-Earth-orbit micro-satellite constellations, assuming operational command risks creating critical tactical blind spots.
A parallel fragility haunts the paradox of South Korea’s defense industry (K-Defense). Despite remarkable global export surges, ranking 10th worldwide with a US$47.6 billion defense budget in 2024, South Korea’s military technology supply chain remains tightly tethered to US licensing.
A staggering 86% of South Korea’s total arms imports between 2020 and 2024 originated from the United States, while flagship platforms such as the KF-21 fighter jet and FA-50 light attack aircraft rely heavily on Washington-licensed engines and components.
International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) grant Washington effective veto power over South Korean arms exports; true industrial self-reliance thus requires aggressive domestic component substitution and supply chain diversification toward NATO partners.
At the strategic level, the conventional Three-Axis System and the ultra-heavy Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile reveal structural limitations when confronting a nuclear-armed adversary. The potential for preemptive escalation from Pyongyang makes conventional deterrence inadequate to guarantee absolute security.
While public opinion polls indicate 76% of South Koreans support developing an independent nuclear capability, backing among strategic experts hovers at just 30–40%, reflecting fears of international sanctions and economic isolation.
Consequently, the most pragmatic path for Seoul is pursuing “nuclear hedging”, drastically shortening its breakout time by developing civilian uranium enrichment and spent fuel reprocessing capabilities.

deduped_items.summary: US President Donald Trump’s abrupt directive on August 16, 2026, to drastically scale back the joint “Ulchi Freedom Shield” (UFS) military exercises sent shockwaves across the Asia-Pacific geostrategic landscape. The unilateral announcement, posted to social media mere hours before the large-scale maneuvers involving 18,000 South Korean troops were set to launch, was justified by Washington […] The post The geopolitical imperative for a self-reliant South Korea appeared first on Asia Times.
deduped_items.body_text:
US President Donald Trump’s abrupt directive on August 16, 2026, to drastically scale back the joint “Ulchi Freedom Shield” (UFS) military exercises sent shockwaves across the Asia-Pacific geostrategic landscape.
The unilateral announcement, posted to social media mere hours before the large-scale maneuvers involving 18,000 South Korean troops were set to launch, was justified by Washington on grounds of cost efficiency, claims of a close personal rapport with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and executive frustration over South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s refusal to commit Seoul’s military to denuclearization operations against Iran.
This transactional and unilateral maneuver directly fractures the foundation of the US-led extended deterrence doctrine, which has served as the bedrock of stability on the Korean Peninsula for over seven decades.
When a nation’s security guarantees can be summarily revoked to accommodate Washington’s domestic political calculus, absolute reliance on the American defense umbrella ceases to be a protective asset. Instead, it becomes an existential vulnerability threatening national survival.
This new geostrategic reality compels South Korea to face an unavoidable historical crossroads. Discourse surrounding strategic autonomy has shifted radically: transitioning from a progressive academic debate into an urgent geopolitical imperative to safeguard national sovereignty against the erratic behavior of its principal ally.
The American dilemma
Washington’s unilateral decree demands an accelerated transfer of Wartime Operational Control (OPCON) to the South Korean military. Although evaluations for Full Operational Capability (FOC) are slated for completion in 2026, severe systemic gaps in intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) integration continue to cast a long shadow over Seoul.
Limitations in independent satellite monitoring to track North Korea’s highly mobile missile launchers and subterranean installations leave South Korea heavily dependent on Washington’s early-warning satellite network.
Without integrating AI-driven automated target recognition and rapidly deploying low-Earth-orbit micro-satellite constellations, assuming operational command risks creating critical tactical blind spots.
A parallel fragility haunts the paradox of South Korea’s defense industry (K-Defense). Despite remarkable global export surges, ranking 10th worldwide with a US$47.6 billion defense budget in 2024, South Korea’s military technology supply chain remains tightly tethered to US licensing.
A staggering 86% of South Korea’s total arms imports between 2020 and 2024 originated from the United States, while flagship platforms such as the KF-21 fighter jet and FA-50 light attack aircraft rely heavily on Washington-licensed engines and components.
International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) grant Washington effective veto power over South Korean arms exports; true industrial self-reliance thus requires aggressive domestic component substitution and supply chain diversification toward NATO partners.
At the strategic level, the conventional Three-Axis System and the ultra-heavy Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile reveal structural limitations when confronting a nuclear-armed adversary. The potential for preemptive escalation from Pyongyang makes conventional deterrence inadequate to guarantee absolute security.
While public opinion polls indicate 76% of South Koreans support developing an independent nuclear capability, backing among strategic experts hovers at just 30–40%, reflecting fears of international sanctions and economic isolation.
Consequently, the most pragmatic path for Seoul is pursuing “nuclear hedging”, drastically shortening its breakout time by developing civilian uranium enrichment and spent fuel reprocessing capabilities.

deduped_items.title: مباشر - النيجر: المجلس العسكري يعلن "استعادة السيطرة تدريجيا" على الوضع
deduped_items.summary: أعلن المجلس العسكري الحاكم في النيجر، الجمعة، "استعادة السيطرة تدريجيا" على الوضع بوجه ما وصفهم "متمردين احتجزوا" جنودا في القاعدة العسكرية الواقعة في محيط مطار نيامي. ودعت السلطات في بيان يحمل توقيع وزير الدفاع الجنرال ساليفو مودي، السكان إلى "الحفاظ على الهدوء ومواصلة أشغالهم بحرية". وكانت حكومة النيجر قالت في وقت سابق، إن قوات ‌الأمن تنتشر إثر سماع دوي إطلاق نار غزير وانفجارات، في حين توقف بث التلفزيون الوطني النيجري وحلت شاشة سوداء في الساعة 9:00 (8:00 ت غ) محل برامج "تلفزيون الساحل".

deduped_items.title: Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche: Beyond sorrow
deduped_items.summary: On the sidelines of the 2026 Rimini Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples, Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche, who have come to be known as “sisters in sorrow", speak to Vatican News about the tragedy that unites them. Roseline is the sister of Fr Jacques Hamel, the French priest who was killed while celebrating Mass in a terrorist attack in 2016. Nassera is the mother of one of the two teenagers who perpetrated the attack and was subsequently shot dead by police. Read all

deduped_items.summary: On the sidelines of the 2026 Rimini Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples, Roseline Hamel and Nassera Kermiche, who have come to be known as “sisters in sorrow", speak to Vatican News about the tragedy that unites them. Roseline is the sister of Fr Jacques Hamel, the French priest who was killed while celebrating Mass in a terrorist attack in 2016. Nassera is the mother of one of the two teenagers who perpetrated the attack and was subsequently shot dead by police. Read all

deduped_items.title: CIA and Vatican visits converge in Moscow amid rising tensions over Ukraine
deduped_items.summary: VATICAN CITY (RNS) — As the CIA director quietly carried warnings to Moscow, Pope Leo’s foreign minister arrived offering dialogue and humanitarian cooperation — two contrasting missions that one Vatican expert likened to a 'good cop, bad cop operation.'
